tagline: From a mountain pass to river junctions and mining towns
intro: US 93 crosses Lost Trail Pass at 7,014 feet on the Idaho-Montana border, then descends beside the North Fork of the Salmon River. At North Fork, the main Salmon turns west while US 93 connects south to Salmon. The Salmon River Scenic Byway uses US 93 and Idaho 75 between Salmon and Stanley.

In 1805, the Lewis and Clark Expedition followed the Salmon River through the site of present-day Salmon, then ascended its north fork toward Montana. Later settlements included Custer, established in 1877, and Clayton, founded as a smelter site in 1881. The Salmon River is also known as the River of No Return.

From Lost Trail Pass, descend to North Fork and continue south through Salmon toward Challis. The junction with Idaho 75 lies south of Challis. Turn toward Clayton, which stands beside the Salmon River between Challis and Stanley. The drive ends at Stanley in the Sawtooth Valley.

moments.title: North Fork
moments.text: Two rivers approaching from opposite directions meet at North Fork. The tributary flows south; the main Salmon arrives from the south and turns almost at a right angle to head west across Idaho. The community takes its name from that confluence. US 93 connects it with Lost Trail Pass to the north and Salmon to the south. Lewis and Clark traveled through the area, ascending the north fork toward Montana. Beyond the turn, the main river enters over 200 miles of continuous canyons through the Salmon River and Clearwater mountains.

moments.title: Clayton
moments.text: Clayton began in 1881 as a place to smelt ore from nearby mines. The town stands beside the Salmon River on Idaho 75, between Challis and Stanley. The Clayton Silver Mine was discovered in 1877, but development remained sporadic until the Clark Mining Company began prospecting in 1927. It operated largely from 1935 to 1986. Low metal prices ended operations, although mineralized ground remained when the mine closed. The Clayton mine produced silver, lead, zinc, copper and gold during those operating years. Clayton’s population was ten at the 2020 census.

moments.title: Custer
moments.text: Custer lies along Yankee Fork Road at 6,470 feet, southwest of Challis. Established in 1877, the ghost town became a National Register historic district in 1981. Seven buildings within the 29-acre district retain enough historic integrity to qualify as contributing properties. Most of Custer belongs to Land of the Yankee Fork State Park, which also includes the nearby historic gold dredge.
